clinician.trajectory_summary: A 49-year-old female of African origin presented to the neurosurgical clinic with a longstanding scalp mass present for more than 10 years. The mass was initially small and non-progressive. It was excised at a peripheral center 5 months prior without histopathological examination. The lesion subsequently recurred and enlarged gradually over 5 months, developing ulceration and bleeding tendency. On physical examination at the neurosurgical clinic, two distinct masses were identified on the right scalp: a larger fungating mass measuring 9×7 cm that was tender, prone to bleeding, and mildly mobile, and a smaller non-fungating lesion measuring 3×3 cm. Routine laboratory studies including CBC and serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Imaging studies (CT head and neck and MRI spine) revealed a multilobulated hyperdense ulcerative scalp lesion on the right frontal region (9×7.8×6 cm) without skull bone erosion or intracranial extension, but with enlarged bilateral cervical lymph nodes at levels I and II and a pathological compression fracture of the T10 vertebral body suspicious for vertebral metastasis. A biopsy was performed confirming the diagnosis of mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Surgical excision was subsequently performed. At 8-month follow-up post-excision, the patient showed no clinical signs of recurrence, no central nervous system symptoms, and the pathological vertebral fracture remained stable without requiring surgical intervention.
